nodes.name: Clergyman
nodes.description: The clergyman was one of the signatories of Marley's burial register.

nodes.name: Clerk
nodes.description: The clerk was one of the signatories of Marley's burial register. | The clerk is an employee of Scrooge who is described as cold but warmer than Scrooge, returning greetings cordially. He earns fifteen shillings a week and has a wife and family. | An employee at the counting-house who is given Christmas day off, goes down a slide, and runs home to Camden Town.

nodes.name: Undertaker
nodes.description: The undertaker was one of the signatories of Marley's burial register.

nodes.name: Chief Mourner
nodes.description: The chief mourner was one of the signatories of Marley's burial register.

nodes.name: Scrooge and Marley
nodes.description: Scrooge and Marley is the name of the firm that was known after Marley's death, with the name never being painted out. | Scrooge and Marley is the firm name displayed above the warehouse door, reflecting the partnership between Scrooge and the deceased Marley.

nodes.name: Hamlet's Father
nodes.description: Hamlet's father is a character from Shakespeare's play who died before the play begins, used as a comparison to emphasize the certainty of Marley's death.

nodes.name: St. Paul's Churchyard
nodes.description: St. Paul's Churchyard is a breezy spot mentioned as a setting for a hypothetical stroll by a middle-aged gentleman.

nodes.name: Paul's Churchyard
nodes.description: Paul's Churchyard is a location referenced as an example of a place that might astonish Scrooge's son's weak mind.

nodes.name: Warehouse Door
nodes.description: The warehouse door is part of the business premises, above which the name 'Scrooge and Marley' is displayed.

nodes.name: The City Clocks
nodes.description: The City Clocks are timekeeping devices in the city that indicate it is three o'clock in the afternoon on Christmas Eve.

nodes.name: Fog
nodes.description: Fog is a dense atmospheric condition that envelops the streets and buildings on Christmas Eve, contributing to the gloomy setting. | The fog is a dense fog that envelops the city on Christmas Eve, making the houses opposite appear as mere phantoms and pouring in through chinks and keyholes. | Fog is a weather condition present in the scene, contributing to the cold and frosty atmosphere.

nodes.name: Counting-House
nodes.description: The Counting-House is Scrooge's workplace, where he sits busy on Christmas Eve, reflecting his dedication to business over personal connections. | The counting-house is Scrooge's place of business where he sits busy on Christmas Eve. It has a door open to keep an eye on the clerk, and it contains a fire and a coal-box. | A business office where Scrooge works and shuts up at the end of the day. | The counting-house is the place of business associated with Scrooge and Marley, which the Ghost's spirit never roved beyond during life.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Clerk
nodes.description: The clerk is an employee in Scrooge's counting-house, working in a small cell copying letters. He has a very small fire and tries to warm himself at a candle. | Scrooge's clerk is an employee of Scrooge, mentioned in Scrooge's wish to speak to him.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Nephew
nodes.description: Scrooge's nephew is a cheerful young man who visits Scrooge on Christmas Eve and greets him with 'A merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!' He is described as having a ruddy and handsome face. | Scrooge's nephew is a character who is cheerful and merry, and he visits Scrooge to wish him a Merry Christmas. | Scrooge's nephew is a kind and generous character who advocates for the true spirit of Christmas, emphasizing its potential for goodwill and human connection. | Scrooge's nephew is a cheerful and persistent character who invites his uncle to dine with him on Christmas, despite his uncle's refusal. | Scrooge's nephew is a cheerful individual who greets Scrooge with Christmas and New Year wishes, and treats the clerk cordially. | Scrooge's nephew, named Fred, is a jovial man who laughs heartily and celebrates Christmas with his wife and friends, and he criticizes Scrooge for calling Christmas a humbug. | Scrooge's nephew is Fred, a character who defends Scrooge and jokes about his beliefs regarding Christmas. | Scrooge's nephew is a relative of Scrooge who expresses pity rather than anger toward Scrooge, noting that Scrooge suffers from his own whims and misses out on a good dinner. | Scrooge's nephew is a good-natured individual who enjoys laughing and is determined to give Scrooge a chance every year, despite Scrooge's attitude. | Scrooge's nephew is the person who visits Uncle Scrooge every year, expressing goodwill and hoping to influence him positively. | Scrooge's nephew is a character who is part of the party and is implied to be in collusion with Topper regarding Topper's pretended blindness. | Scrooge's nephew is a character who hosts the games and finds amusement in Scrooge's participation.

nodes.name: Christmas
nodes.description: Christmas is an annual holiday that Scrooge criticizes as a humbug and a time of financial burden and aging. | Christmas is a holiday that Scrooge despises and his nephew cherishes, seen as a time for kindness and charity. | Christmas is the time of year when the charitable gentlemen choose to collect donations for the poor. | Christmas is the season during which the events of the story take place. | Christmas is the festive occasion during which the Cratchit family celebrates with a toast and blessings. | Christmas is a holiday that Scrooge dismisses as a humbug, sparking discussion among his relatives. | Christmas is a holiday that is central to the conversation, with Scrooge's nephew determined to visit Scrooge every year regardless of Scrooge's reaction. | Christmas is an annual holiday celebrated with family gatherings, games, and music. | Christmas is a holiday celebrated with merriment and goodwill, and the narrative suggests that the holiday season seems condensed into the time Scrooge spends with the Ghost. | The Christmas season is referenced as a background event during the family gathering. | Christmas is the holiday that Scrooge celebrates joyfully, reflecting his newfound spirit of generosity. | Christmas is a holiday that Scrooge is said to know how to keep well.

nodes.name: Frost
nodes.description: Frost is a weather condition present in the scene, contributing to the cold atmosphere.

nodes.name: The Clerk
nodes.description: The clerk is an employee in Scrooge's office who involuntarily applauds the nephew's speech, then suppresses his enthusiasm out of fear of Scrooge's reaction. | The clerk works for Scrooge and is poorly dressed for winter. He celebrates Christmas Eve by sliding on Cornhill and playing blind man's-buff at home in Camden Town.

nodes.name: Bedlam
nodes.description: Bedlam is referenced by Scrooge as a place he would retire to, implying a mental asylum, used metaphorically to express his disdain for the clerk's Christmas cheer.

nodes.name: Portly Gentlemen
nodes.description: The portly gentlemen are two pleasant visitors who enter Scrooge's office after his nephew leaves, carrying books and papers, and address the firm as Scrooge and Marley's.

nodes.name: Scrooge and Marley's
nodes.description: Scrooge and Marley's is the name of the business firm, as referred to by the portly gentlemen. | Scrooge and Marley's is the counting-house where Scrooge works, as referenced by The Gentleman when he identifies Scrooge.

nodes.name: Mr. Marley
nodes.description: Mr. Marley is a deceased partner of Scrooge, having been dead for seven years, as stated by Scrooge. | Mr. Marley is the deceased business partner of Mr. Scrooge, mentioned as having died seven years prior.

nodes.name: Mr. Scrooge
nodes.description: Mr. Scrooge is a character who is questioned by a gentleman about his identity and expresses skepticism about provisions for the poor. | Mr. Scrooge is described as an odious, stingy, hard, and unfeeling man, and is considered the Ogre of the Cratchit family.

nodes.name: The Gentleman
nodes.description: The Gentleman is a visitor who seeks donations for the poor and destitute during the festive season. | The Gentleman is a person who, along with others, is trying to raise funds to provide the poor with necessities and discusses their cause with Scrooge. | The Gentleman is a portly, good-natured individual who had visited Scrooge's counting-house the previous day to collect a charitable donation, and is now greeted warmly by Scrooge. | The gentleman is a person who initially addresses Scrooge, is surprised by Scrooge's offer, and agrees to visit Scrooge after shaking hands with him.

nodes.name: The Poor Law
nodes.description: The Poor Law is a system of legislation in operation that Mr. Scrooge references in his inquiry about provisions for the poor.

nodes.name: The Union Workhouses
nodes.description: The Union workhouses are institutions that are still in operation, as mentioned by the gentleman.

nodes.name: The Treadmill
nodes.description: The Treadmill is a punitive device referenced by Mr. Scrooge in his questioning of social provisions.

nodes.name: Treadmill
nodes.description: The Treadmill is a penal institution or device that is in full operation, as referenced in the conversation.

nodes.name: Poor Law
nodes.description: The Poor Law is a legal and administrative system providing relief for the poor, which Scrooge supports and which is in full operation.

nodes.name: Want
nodes.description: Want refers to poverty and necessity, which is keenly felt during Christmas time. | Want is a girl who symbolizes the societal ill of poverty and need.

nodes.name: Abundance
nodes.description: Abundance refers to wealth and plenty, which is contrasted with Want during the holiday season.

nodes.name: Gentlemen
nodes.description: The gentlemen are visitors who approach Scrooge with a charitable purpose but withdraw when Scrooge rejects them.

nodes.name: Lord Mayor
nodes.description: The Lord Mayor is a high-ranking official who orders his household to celebrate Christmas in a grand manner. | A person in the stronghold of Mansion House who gave orders to his fifty cooks and butlers to celebrate Christmas appropriately.

nodes.name: Little Tailor
nodes.description: The little tailor is a man who was fined by the Lord Mayor for being drunk and bloodthirsty, but still prepares for Christmas. | A tailor who was fined by the Lord Mayor for being drunk and bloodthirsty, and who stirs up tomorrow's pudding in preparation for Christmas.

nodes.name: Mansion House
nodes.description: The Mansion House is the official residence of the Lord Mayor. | A stronghold that serves as the residence of the Lord Mayor, where the Christmas orders are given.

nodes.name: St. Dunstan
nodes.description: A person of legendary status who is referenced in relation to the cold weather and his potential interaction with the Evil Spirit.

nodes.name: Christmas Carol
nodes.description: A song sung by a singer at Scrooge's keyhole, but the singer flees in terror when Scrooge seizes a ruler. | Christmas carol is a song sung by a boy at Scrooge's door, which Scrooge regrets not rewarding.

nodes.name: The Singer
nodes.description: A person who sings a Christmas carol at Scrooge's keyhole and flees in terror when Scrooge reacts aggressively.

nodes.name: Camden Town
nodes.description: The destination of the clerk's run home after work. | Camden Town is the neighborhood where the clerk lives and returns to celebrate Christmas Eve. | Camden Town is the destination for the turkey, where Scrooge intends to have it delivered.

nodes.name: Chambers
nodes.description: Chambers are a gloomy suite of rooms in a lowering pile of building where Scrooge lives, once belonging to his deceased partner, Marley. | Chambers are Scrooge's dusty living quarters, where he spends time alone.

nodes.name: The Knocker
nodes.description: The knocker on Scrooge's door is large and unremarkable, but it transforms into Marley's face. | The knocker is a door knocker that Scrooge admires, noting its honest expression and calling it wonderful.

nodes.name: Marley's Face
nodes.description: Marley's Face appears on the knocker with a dismal light, resembling a bad lobster in a dark cellar.

nodes.name: Genius of the Weather
nodes.description: The Genius of the Weather is a mythical figure imagined to sit in mournful meditation on the threshold of Scrooge's house.

nodes.name: City of London
nodes.description: The City of London is the area where Scrooge is known to have little fancy about him, compared to its officials.

nodes.name: The Door Knocker
nodes.description: The Door Knocker is a physical object on Scrooge's door that briefly transforms into Marley's face.

nodes.name: The House
nodes.description: The house is the setting where the story unfolds, with multiple floors and a cellar containing wine-merchant's casks, and a staircase wide enough for a hearse.

nodes.name: Echoes
nodes.description: Echoes are sounds that resound through the house, which Scrooge is not frightened by.

nodes.name: Wine-Merchant's Cellars
nodes.description: The wine-merchant's cellars are located below the house, contributing to the echoes.

nodes.name: Staircase
nodes.description: The staircase is wide enough to accommodate a hearse, indicating its large size.

nodes.name: Hearse
nodes.description: A hearse is a vehicle that could easily be driven up the staircase, as imagined by the narrator.

nodes.name: Sitting-Room
nodes.description: The sitting-room is one of the rooms Scrooge inspects, contains a table, sofa, fire, spoon, and basin. | The sitting-room is the location where Scrooge expresses his joy and interacts with household items after his transformation.

nodes.name: Bedroom
nodes.description: The bedroom is one of the rooms Scrooge inspects, contains a bed he checks under.

nodes.name: Lumber-Room
nodes.description: The lumber-room is a storage room that Scrooge checks, and it appears as usual.

nodes.name: Candle
nodes.description: A candle is Scrooge's source of light as he walks up the stairs.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.description: A small fire in the grate that Scrooge sits close to in an attempt to warm himself on a bitter night.

nodes.name: Gruel
nodes.description: Gruel is a simple porridge-like food that Scrooge prepares and consumes, situated in a saucepan on the hob.

nodes.name: Dressing-Gown
nodes.description: A dressing-gown hanging in a suspicious attitude, which Scrooge later puts on.

nodes.name: Dutch Tiles
nodes.description: Quaint tiles in the fireplace depicting biblical scenes, which distract Scrooge's thoughts.

nodes.name: Bell
nodes.description: A disused bell in the room that begins to swing, causing Scrooge astonishment and dread. | A disused bell in Scrooge's room that begins to swing and ring loudly, signaling the ghost's arrival.

nodes.name: Heavy Chain
nodes.description: A heavy chain dragged by Marley's Ghost, making a clanking noise as it moves through the house.

nodes.name: Haunted House
nodes.description: The building where Scrooge lives, which is described as haunted and where the supernatural events occur.

nodes.name: Cellar
nodes.description: The wine-merchant's cellar, from which the clanking noise originates before the ghost ascends.

nodes.name: Jacob Marley
nodes.description: Jacob Marley is the ghost of Scrooge's former business partner, appearing in chains and transparent form, and insists on being addressed as his former self. | Jacob Marley is the ghost of Scrooge's former business partner. He appears to Scrooge to reveal his identity and engage in a conversation about the reality of his presence. | Jacob Marley is the ghost of Scrooge's former business partner, who wears a heavy chain forged in life. | Jacob Marley is a deceased former business partner of Ebenezer Scrooge, appearing as a ghost who is condemned to wander in perpetual remorse. | Jacob Marley is the ghost of Scrooge's former business partner, who appears to warn Scrooge about his fate. | Jacob Marley is the deceased partner who arranged for the second messenger to visit Scrooge. | Jacob Marley is a deceased former business partner of Scrooge, mentioned in relation to the sexton's spade. | Jacob Marley is a deceased associate of Scrooge whose prediction about the spirits is remembered by Scrooge. | Jacob Marley is mentioned by Scrooge in a prayer of gratitude, indicating a past connection and influence. | Jacob Marley is a deceased business partner of Scrooge, referenced by Scrooge in a moment of gratitude.

nodes.name: Ghost Of Marley
nodes.description: The ghost of Marley is a supernatural being, transparent and wearing chains, who appears before Scrooge to convey a warning.

nodes.name: Chain
nodes.description: The chain is clasped about Marley's middle, made of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel, symbolizing Marley's earthly attachments.

spirit condemned to wander the earth and witness what it cannot share. | The Ghost is the spectral apparition of Jacob Marley, conveying messages from other regions and speaking of its own torment and nodes.name: The Chain
nodes.description: The Chain is a symbolic object that represents the burdens and consequences of a life lived without compassion. | The Chain is a physical object carried by Marley's ghost, symbolizing his burden and past misdeeds.

nodes.name: The Ward
nodes.description: The Ward is implied as a legal jurisdiction or location where proceedings might be justified regarding the Ghost's noise.

nodes.name: Mankind
nodes.description: Mankind represents humanity and the common welfare, which Marley claims was his true business.

nodes.name: The Star
nodes.description: The Star is a celestial object that guided the Wise Men, symbolizing hope and spiritual guidance.

nodes.name: Three Spirits
nodes.description: Three Spirits are supernatural entities that will visit Scrooge on consecutive nights as part of his chance to escape the Ghost's fate.

nodes.name: Penance
nodes.description: Penance is described as a significant part of the Ghost's punishment and the reason for its visit to warn Scrooge.

nodes.name: Chance and Hope
nodes.description: Chance and hope refer to the possibility of Scrooge escaping the Ghost's fate through the visits of the Three Spirits.

nodes.name: Phantoms
nodes.description: Phantoms are supernatural beings wandering in the air, wearing chains like Marley's Ghost, moaning, and unable to interfere in human matters.

nodes.name: Chains
nodes.description: Chains are worn by Marley's Ghost and other phantoms as symbols of their imprisonment.

nodes.name: Illustration
nodes.description: An illustration depicts the air filled with phantoms wandering in restless haste and moaning.

nodes.name: Spirit Voices
nodes.description: Spirit Voices are the ethereal voices of the ghosts that fade away together with them.

nodes.name: Ghost In A White Waistcoat
nodes.description: A ghost in a white waistcoat with an iron safe attached to its ankle, who laments being unable to assist a woman with an infant.

nodes.name: Iron Safe
nodes.description: An iron safe is attached to the ankle of one ghost, symbolizing a burden.

nodes.name: The Invisible World
nodes.description: The Invisible World is a realm of spirits and ghosts that Scrooge glimpses.

nodes.name: Wretched Woman
nodes.description: A woman with an infant, seen below on a doorstep, whom the ghost in the white waistcoat wishes to assist.

nodes.name: The Clock
nodes.description: The Clock is a heavy bell-driven clock in Scrooge's room that unexpectedly continues ringing up to twelve, which Scrooge believes is wrong, possibly due to an icicle in the works.

nodes.name: The Repeater
nodes.description: The Repeater is Scrooge's pocket watch that also strikes twelve, causing him further confusion about the time.

nodes.name: An Icicle
nodes.description: An icicle is suggested by Scrooge as a possible cause of the clock malfunctioning.

nodes.name: The Sun
nodes.description: The Sun is mentioned by Scrooge as a possible element affected by unusual time, as he wonders if twelve could be noon.

nodes.name: The Weather
nodes.description: The Weather is characterized by fog and extreme cold, which affects Scrooge's perception and actions at the window.

nodes.name: First of Exchange
nodes.description: The First of Exchange is a financial document mentioned in Scrooge's thoughts, illustrating his confusion about time and its passage.

nodes.name: United States Security
nodes.description: A United States security is a financial instrument that would be of diminished value without a count of days, as referenced in Scrooge's musings.

nodes.name: The Spirit
nodes.description: The Spirit is a ghostly figure that appears to Scrooge, characterized by its ever-changing form, white hair, and a bright light from its head. | The Spirit is a supernatural figure who sprinkles water and incense on dinners using a torch, and interacts with Scrooge during Christmas celebrations. | The Spirit is a ghostly figure that quotes Scrooge's own words back to him, rebuking him for his callous attitude toward the poor. | The Spirit is a supernatural being guiding Scrooge on a journey to observe Christmas scenes. | The Spirit is a supernatural being that shows Scrooge the children Ignorance and Want and speaks of their significance. | The Spirit is a phantom guide that leads Scrooge through scenes and points to people, providing explanation. | The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come, who guides Scrooge through possible future scenes. | The Spirit is a supernatural guide accompanying Scrooge during the vision. | The Spirit is a supernatural being guiding Scrooge through the vision, pointing towards a churchyard and a specific grave. | A spectral entity that shows the protagonist his past, present, and future, and responds to his pleas for redemption. | The Spirit is a spectral entity that Scrooge encounters, which repulses him and eventually dwindles into a bedpost.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Bedroom
nodes.description: Scrooge's bedroom is the setting where the supernatural encounter occurs.

nodes.name: The Curtains
nodes.description: The curtains of Scrooge's bed are drawn aside by the Spirit.

nodes.name: The Holly Branch
nodes.description: The Holly Branch is a branch of fresh green holly held by the Spirit.

nodes.name: The Country Road
nodes.description: The country road is a location where Scrooge and the Ghost arrive, evoking Scrooge's childhood memories.

nodes.name: Market-Town
nodes.description: A little market-town visible in the distance with a bridge, church, and winding river, where Scrooge spent his childhood.

nodes.name: Winter Day
nodes.description: A clear, cold winter day with snow on the ground, marking the setting of Scrooge's childhood memory.

nodes.name: Odours
nodes.description: A thousand scents associated with thoughts, hopes, joys, and cares from Scrooge's past, triggering memories.

nodes.name: Boys
nodes.description: A group of boys riding ponies and in carts, shouting and in high spirits, representing Christmas cheer in Scrooge's past. | Boys are the children who delight in watching snow fall from rooftops and creating artificial snowstorms.

nodes.name: The School
nodes.description: The School is a large, decaying mansion where a solitary child is left neglected by friends. | The school is the location of Scrooge's childhood memories, where he is greeted by the schoolmaster.

nodes.name: The Travellers
nodes.description: The Travellers are a group of joyful boys who celebrate Christmas and are known by Scrooge.

nodes.name: The Mansion
nodes.description: The Mansion is a dull red brick building with a cupola and bell, in a state of decay, representing the school. | The mansion is a large, decaying brick house that is the setting of the scene, showing signs of neglect.

nodes.name: Young Scrooge
nodes.description: Young Scrooge is the childhood version of Scrooge, shown as a lonely boy reading in a barren classroom.

nodes.name: Ali Baba
nodes.description: Ali Baba is a fictional character from a story that appears outside the window, bringing joy to young Scrooge. | Ali Baba is a character from the story 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves', mentioned by Scrooge as a dear old character.

nodes.name: The Classroom
nodes.description: The classroom is a long, bare room with desks and forms, where young Scrooge is found reading by the fire.

nodes.name: The Poplar Tree
nodes.description: The poplar tree is a despondent, leafless tree in the yard, its sighs affecting Scrooge's emotions.

nodes.name: The Ass
nodes.description: The ass is a donkey laden with wood, led by Ali Baba outside the window.

nodes.name: Valentine
nodes.description: Valentine is a character, presumably from a story, who is brother to Orson.

nodes.name: Orson
nodes.description: Orson is a character, described as Valentine's wild brother.

nodes.name: Sultan's Groom
nodes.description: The Sultan's Groom is a character who was turned upside down by the Genii.

nodes.name: Genii
nodes.description: The Genii are supernatural beings who turned the Sultan's Groom upside down.

nodes.name: Princess
nodes.description: The Princess is a character who was married to the Sultan's Groom.

nodes.name: Parrot
nodes.description: The Parrot is a green and yellow bird with a lettuce-like growth on its head, called 'Poor Robin Crusoe' by its owner. | The parrot is a speaking bird that calls out to Robin Crusoe, as quoted in the text.

nodes.name: Robin Crusoe
nodes.description: Robin Crusoe is a fictional character who sailed around an island and returned home. | Robin Crusoe is a character referenced by the parrot in a dialogue, about whom the parrot asks where he has been after sailing around the island.

nodes.name: Friday
nodes.description: Friday is a character who runs for his life to a little creek. | Friday is a character who runs for his life to a little creek, as mentioned in the text.

nodes.name: Ghost

nodes.name: The Schoolmaster

nodes.name: Scrooge's Room
nodes.description: The room where Scrooge is staying, with panels and windows that deteriorate.

nodes.name: Scrooge's School
nodes.description: The school Scrooge attends, from which he is taken home.

nodes.name: The Hall
nodes.description: The hall where the schoolmaster appears and calls for Scrooge's box.

nodes.name: Master Scrooge
nodes.description: Master Scrooge is the younger version of Scrooge, seen in a childhood memory at school.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Sister
nodes.description: Scrooge's sister is a delicate but warm-hearted child who embraces her brother and takes him home.

nodes.name: The Nephew
nodes.description: The Nephew is revealed to be the child of Scrooge's sister. | The Nephew is the host at the house and is in the dining-room with his wife when Scrooge visits.

nodes.name: The City
nodes.description: The city is a bustling place with shops and streets, where Scrooge and the Ghost observe Christmas-time evening. | The city is the location towards which the Spirit stretches his hand, representing society that slanders those who speak of the children. | The City is the location where Scrooge and the Spirit move, appearing to spring up around them as they travel. | The City is the setting where Scrooge and the Phantom appear, surrounded by merchants and business activity.

nodes.name: The Warehouse
nodes.description: The warehouse is a location the Ghost stops at, asking Scrooge if he knows it. | The warehouse is the place where Scrooge was apprenticed and where he revisits his past with the Ghost. | The warehouse is the workplace owned by Fezziwig, which is cleared and transformed into a ball-room for the Christmas Eve celebration.

nodes.name: Old Fezziwig
nodes.description: Old Fezziwig is a cheerful old gentleman in a Welsh wig, a former employer of Scrooge, who is seen sitting behind a high desk and calls out to his apprentices. | Old Fezziwig is a character who hosts a dance and leads the festivities, including dancing with Mrs. Fezziwig.

nodes.name: Dick

nodes.name: Ebenezer
nodes.description: Ebenezer is an apprentice of Fezziwig, addressed cheerfully during the Christmas Eve preparations.

nodes.name: Warehouse
nodes.description: The warehouse is the venue transformed into a ballroom for the Christmas party hosted by Fezziwig.

nodes.name: Fiddler
nodes.description: The fiddler provides music for the dance, using the desk as an orchestra, and plays energetically.

nodes.name: Miss Fezziwigs
nodes.description: The three Miss Fezziwigs are the daughters of Fezziwig, beaming and lovable.

nodes.name: Young Followers
nodes.description: The six young followers are young men whose hearts were broken by the Miss Fezziwigs.

nodes.name: Young Men and Women
nodes.description: The young men and women employed in the business attend the party and participate in the dancing.

nodes.name: Housemaid
nodes.description: The housemaid is a servant who attends the party with her cousin, the baker.

nodes.name: Baker
nodes.description: The baker is the cousin of the housemaid, attending the party.

nodes.name: Cook
nodes.description: The cook is a servant who attends with her brother's particular friend, the milkman.

nodes.name: Milkman
nodes.description: The milkman is the friend of the cook's brother, attending the party.

nodes.name: Boy from Over the Way
nodes.description: The boy from over the way is suspected of not having enough board from his master and hides behind the girl from next door.

nodes.name: Girl from Next Door
nodes.description: The girl from next door is proved to have had her ears pulled by her mistress.

nodes.name: Christmas Party
nodes.description: A festive dance held in the warehouse, hosted by Fezziwig, featuring music and dancing.

nodes.name: Music-Book
nodes.description: The music-book is used by the fiddler to play tunes at the party.

nodes.name: The Fiddler
nodes.description: The fiddler is a musician who plays music for the dances, including 'Sir Roger de Coverley', and is described as an 'artful dog'.

nodes.name: Sir Roger de Coverley
nodes.description: Sir Roger de Coverley is a dance tune played by the fiddler during the evening.

nodes.name: The Dance
nodes.description: The dance is a social gathering where numerous couples dance various figures, including the top couple's leads.

nodes.name: Domestic Ball
nodes.description: A festive ball hosted by the Fezziwigs, featuring dancing and merry interactions, ending at eleven o'clock.

nodes.name: The Two Apprentices
nodes.description: The two apprentices are Fezziwig's current apprentices who express gratitude and praise for Fezziwig.

nodes.name: The Party
nodes.description: The party is a Christmas event hosted by Fezziwig, where he bids farewell to guests and receives praise from his apprentices.

nodes.name: Fair Young Girl
nodes.description: A fair young girl in mourning dress is seen with a younger Scrooge, indicating a past relationship.

nodes.name: He
nodes.description: He is an older man, showing signs of care and avarice, with an eager and greedy eye. He is engaged in a conversation with a young girl in mourning.

nodes.name: The Young Girl
nodes.description: A fair young girl in mourning dress, with tears in her eyes, speaking softly about being displaced by another idol. | The Young Girl is a beautiful young girl in the scene who resembles the last person Scrooge saw.

nodes.name: The Golden Idol
nodes.description: A metaphorical golden idol representing wealth and greed that has displaced the girl in the man's affections.

nodes.name: Poverty
nodes.description: Poverty is discussed as something the world treats with severity, a condition the man fears.

nodes.name: The Contract
nodes.description: An old contract, made when both were poor, representing their betrothal or agreement to improve their fortune through industry. | An old agreement made when both were poor, intended to improve their fortune through patient industry.

nodes.name: Gain
nodes.description: Gain is the master passion that has engrossed the man, leading to his obsession with wealth.

nodes.name: The Girl
nodes.description: A woman involved in an old romantic contract, now expressing that the nature of the relationship has changed and proposing release.

nodes.name: The Man
nodes.description: A man who was once a boy when the contract was made, now engaged in a conversation about whether he has changed. | The man is a character who, along with Mrs. Dilber, agrees with the woman's statement.

nodes.name: Girl
nodes.description: A woman who has resolved to release her former love from an engagement, citing a change in his nature and principles. | The Girl is one of two children shown to Scrooge, described as wretched and wolfish, symbolizing want.

nodes.name: The Former Love
nodes.description: A man who was once loved by the Girl but now embodies a changed nature, measuring everything by gain.

nodes.name: The Matron
nodes.description: The Matron is a comely matron who sits opposite the young girl, suggesting she is the older version of the girl.

nodes.name: The Daughter
nodes.description: The Daughter is the daughter of the matron and participates in the children's games, getting pillaged by the young brigands.

nodes.name: The Scene
nodes.description: The Scene is a past event showing a comfortable room with a fire, where a family with many children enjoys boisterous games.

nodes.name: The Father
nodes.description: The father is the master of the house who returns home with gifts and is greeted by his family.

nodes.name: The Children
nodes.description: The children are the boisterous group that greets the father and later goes to bed. | The children are descendants of the old man and woman, joining in the Christmas song. | The Children are the mother's children who are playing in the room during the vision.

nodes.name: The Porter
nodes.description: The porter is a man laden with Christmas toys and presents who is mobbed by the children.

nodes.name: Christmas Toys
nodes.description: Christmas toys are the presents brought by the porter and distributed to the children.

nodes.name: Husband
nodes.description: The husband is Belle's spouse who recognizes Scrooge and reports seeing him alone at his office.

nodes.name: The Extinguisher-Cap
nodes.description: The Extinguisher-Cap is a device Scrooge uses in an attempt to suppress the Ghost's light.

nodes.name: The Second Spirit
nodes.description: The Second Spirit is the second messenger sent to Scrooge, expected to appear after the bell strikes One.

nodes.name: The Bell
nodes.description: The Bell is a clock that strikes the hour, signaling the arrival of the spirits.

nodes.name: The Bedroom
nodes.description: The Bedroom is where Scrooge finds himself after the encounter with the Ghost and where he awaits the second spirit.

nodes.name: The Light
nodes.description: The Light is a radiant, ghostly illumination associated with the Ghost and later emanating in Scrooge's room. | The Light is a ruddy glow that surrounds Scrooge, alarming him, and is later revealed to emanate from the adjoining room.

nodes.name: The Room
nodes.description: The Room is Scrooge's own room which has undergone a surprising transformation, adorned with living green and filled with festive foods and a roaring fire. | The room is dark with a bare, uncurtained bed, where the body of the man lies under a ragged sheet.

nodes.name: Living Green
nodes.description: Living green consists of holly, mistletoe, and ivy that hang on the walls and ceiling, reflecting light like mirrors.

nodes.name: Food
nodes.description: A large assortment of food items such as turkeys, geese, game, poultry, brawn, joints of meat, sucking-pigs, sausages, mince-pies, plum-puddings, oysters, chestnuts, apples, oranges, pears, twelfth-cakes, and punch.

nodes.name: Chamber
nodes.description: The chamber is the room where the Ghost of Christmas Present sits in state upon a throne of food, dimmed by the steam from the punch.

nodes.name: Holy Wreath
nodes.description: A wreath made of holly, adorned with shining icicles, worn on the head of the Ghost of Christmas Present.

nodes.name: Antique Sheath
nodes.description: An antique scabbard, rusted and empty, girded around the Ghost's middle, symbolizing peace.

nodes.name: Christmas Morning
nodes.description: Christmas morning is the time setting for the scene described, where people are outdoors in the city streets.

nodes.name: City Streets
nodes.description: City streets are the urban environment where the characters and activities take place on Christmas morning. | The city streets are the initial setting where Scrooge and the Spirit observe festive preparations in houses.

nodes.name: People
nodes.description: People are the residents of the city, engaged in clearing snow and shopping, displaying jovial and eager behavior.

nodes.name: Poulterers' Shops
nodes.description: Poulterers' shops are retail locations selling poultry, still partially open on Christmas morning.

nodes.name: Fruiterers' Shops
nodes.description: Fruiterers' shops are retail locations selling fruits, radiant with displays of chestnuts, Spanish onions, pears, apples, grapes, filberts, and Norfolk Biffins.

nodes.name: Grocers' Shops
nodes.description: Grocers' shops are retail locations offering a wide range of groceries including tea, coffee, raisins, almonds, cinnamon, spices, candied fruits, figs, and French plums, with a bustling atmosphere.

nodes.name: Snow
nodes.description: Snow is the precipitation covering rooftops and ground, being cleared by people and causing a brisk atmosphere.

nodes.name: Mistletoe
nodes.description: Mistletoe is a plant hung up in shops, associated with Christmas decorations and traditions.

nodes.name: Chestnuts
nodes.description: Chestnuts are nuts displayed in large baskets at fruiterers' shops, described with humorous anthropomorphic qualities. | Chestnuts are placed on the fire and sputter and crack noisily as part of the family's Christmas celebration.

nodes.name: Spanish Onions
nodes.description: Spanish onions are a vegetable product in the fruiterers' shops, described with humorous characteristics.

nodes.name: Pears
nodes.description: Pears are fruits displayed in blooming pyramids at the fruiterers' shops.

nodes.name: Apples
nodes.description: Apples are fruits displayed in blooming pyramids at the fruiterers' shops.

nodes.name: Grapes
nodes.description: Grapes are bunches of fruit dangled from hooks at the fruiterers' shops to entice customers.

nodes.name: Filberts
nodes.description: Filberts are nuts piled in the shops, their fragrance evoking walks in the woods.

nodes.name: Norfolk Biffins
nodes.description: Norfolk Biffins are a type of apple, notable for their squab and swarthy appearance, appealing to customers.

nodes.name: Tea
nodes.description: Tea is a beverage ingredient sold in grocers' shops, with a scent that is grateful to the nose.

nodes.name: Coffee
nodes.description: Coffee is a beverage ingredient sold in grocers' shops, with a scent that is grateful to the nose.

nodes.name: Grocer
nodes.description: The grocer is the shopkeeper of the grocers' shop, described as frank and fresh, with polished hearts on their aprons.

nodes.name: The Grocer
nodes.description: The grocer is a shopkeeper who, along with his staff, is described as cheerful and busy during the Christmas season.

nodes.name: Customers
nodes.description: Customers are the people shopping in the grocery store, depicted as hurried and eager, causing commotion in their Christmas preparations.

nodes.name: The Bakers
nodes.description: The bakers are individuals who operate the bakeries where poor revellers send their dinners to be cooked during Christmas.

nodes.name: Christmas Day
nodes.description: Christmas Day is the holiday setting during which the scenes of shopping, cooking, and reconciliation occur. | Christmas Day is the occasion during which the Cratchit family prepares their festive meal and is visited by the Ghost. | Christmas Day is the holiday during which the Cratchit family shares their toast and expresses their feelings about Mr. Scrooge. | Christmas Day is a holiday that is repeatedly mentioned by Bob Cratchit as a reason to temper Mrs. Cratchit's harsh words about Scrooge. | Christmas Day is the holiday that Scrooge discovers it is, bringing him joy and relief.

nodes.name: The Torch
nodes.description: The torch is a special item held by the Spirit that sprinkles water to restore good humor and incense on dinners.

nodes.name: The Seventh Day
nodes.description: The Seventh Day is a concept referring to the Sabbath, which Scrooge accuses the Spirit's name and family of being used to close places of dining, thereby depriving the poor of their means of dining.

nodes.name: Bob Cratchit's Dwelling
nodes.description: Bob Cratchit's Dwelling is the home of Scrooge's clerk, which the Spirit blesses with sprinklings from his torch.

nodes.name: The Poor
nodes.description: The Poor refers to the impoverished individuals who most need kindly given dinners and whose innocent enjoyment is being restricted by the closing of places on the Seventh Day.

nodes.name: Master Peter Cratchit
nodes.description: Master Peter Cratchit is the eldest son of the Cratchit family who tends to the potatoes and is admired by his younger siblings. | Master Peter Cratchit is a son in the Cratchit family who helps fetch the goose and mashes the potatoes.

nodes.name: Cratchit Family
nodes.description: The Cratchit family consists of Bob, Mrs. Cratchit, Belinda, Peter, Tiny Tim, Martha, and two younger children, observed during Christmas preparations. | The Cratchit family is the family unit gathered for a Christmas dinner, including Bob, Mrs. Cratchit, and their children. | The Cratchit family consists of Bob, Mrs. Cratchit, Peter, Tiny Tim, and other children. They are depicted as a close, loving family sharing grief and joy together. | The Cratchit Family includes Bob Cratchit, Mrs. Cratchit, their daughters, the two young Cratchits, and Peter, who all express love and remembrance.

nodes.name: The Two Young Cratchits
nodes.description: Two young children in the Cratchit family who are energetic and participate in the merriment, announcing Martha's arrival and helping Tiny Tim. | The Two Young Cratchits are the younger children of the Cratchit family who help with chores and escort Tiny Tim. | The two young Cratchits are children of the Cratchit family who become livid at the supposition that the pudding might be stolen.

nodes.name: The Cratchit Family
nodes.description: The Cratchit family is a close-knit family celebrating Christmas together, consisting of Bob, Mrs. Cratchit, Tiny Tim, Martha, Peter, Belinda, and the younger children. | The Cratchit family includes Bob, his wife, and their children, including Tiny Tim, Peter, and Martha; they are poor but happy. | The Cratchit family includes the mother, daughters, and sons, who are depicted in a quiet moment.

nodes.name: Cratchit
nodes.description: Cratchit is a family member who prepared the gravy for the goose dinner.

nodes.name: Master Peter
nodes.description: Master Peter is a child in the Cratchit family who mashed the potatoes with great vigour. | Master Peter is the eldest son of the Cratchit family, who contemplates investments from a prospective income.

nodes.name: Miss Belinda
nodes.description: Miss Belinda is a child in the Cratchit family who sweetened the applesauce and later changed the plates.

nodes.name: Martha
nodes.description: Martha is a member of the Cratchit family who dusted the hot plates for the meal. | Martha is a poor apprentice at a milliner's and the daughter of Bob Cratchit, who shares details about her work.

nodes.name: Bob
nodes.description: Bob is a member of the Cratchit family who sat next to Tiny Tim and expressed admiration for the goose. | Bob is a family man who serves hot drinks from a jug, proposes a Christmas toast to his family, and cares deeply for his son Tiny Tim. | Bob is a family man who works and shares news about Mr. Scrooge's nephew's kindness with his family. | Bob is an employee who arrives late and apologizes to Scrooge.

nodes.name: The two young Cratchits
nodes.description: The two young Cratchits are children in the Cratchit family who set chairs and crammed spoons into their mouths, then excited Tiny Tim.

nodes.name: The Goose
nodes.description: The goose is the main dish of the Cratchit family's dinner, praised for its tenderness, flavour, size, and cheapness. | The goose is a food item being eaten by the Cratchit family, and its consumption is part of the context in which the pudding is served.

nodes.name: The Pudding
nodes.description: The pudding is a dessert that Mrs. Cratchit prepared and brought in after the goose, causing anxiety about its condition.

nodes.name: The Christmas Pudding
nodes.description: The Christmas pudding is a dessert made by Mrs. Cratchit, described as speckled, hard, firm, and blazing with brandy and holly.

nodes.name: The Back-Yard Wall
nodes.description: The back-yard wall is the boundary over which someone might have climbed to steal the pudding.

nodes.name: Christmas Pudding
nodes.description: The Christmas pudding is a hard, firm pudding served with ignited brandy and holly, considered a great success by Bob Cratchit.

nodes.name: Christmas Dinner
nodes.description: The Christmas dinner is the occasion during which the Cratchit family gathers and celebrates with pudding and a toast.

nodes.name: The Jug's Compound
nodes.description: The compound in the jug is a drink served to the family, considered perfect after tasting and held in tumblers and a custard cup.

nodes.name: Crutch
nodes.description: A crutch is used by Tiny Tim; in the vision, a crutch without an owner is preserved, symbolizing the child's death.

nodes.name: The Poor Man's Child
nodes.description: The Poor Man's Child is a child mentioned by the Spirit as an example of a life that might be deemed worthless by Scrooge's standards.

nodes.name: The Founder of the Feast
nodes.description: The Founder of the Feast is the title Bob Cratchit gives to Mr. Scrooge during a Christmas toast, despite Scrooge's negative traits.

nodes.name: The Cratchit Children
nodes.description: The Cratchit children participate in the Christmas toast and show a lack of heartiness when drinking to Scrooge's health.

nodes.name: Spirit
nodes.description: The Spirit is a supernatural guide accompanying Scrooge, whose torch sprinkles brightness, making the family appear happier. | The Spirit is a ghostly entity representing the Ghost of the Future, whose presence instills fear in Scrooge and guides him silently. | The Spirit is a phantom that guides Scrooge through the scene. | The Spirit is a supernatural entity that Scrooge confronts, leading to his emotional release and change of heart.

nodes.name: The Song
nodes.description: A song about a lost child travelling in the snow, sung by Tiny Tim.

nodes.name: Moor
nodes.description: The moor is a bleak, desert-like place where miners live and where the Spirit takes Scrooge.

nodes.name: Miners
nodes.description: Miners are people who live in huts on the moor and work underground; they know the Spirit.

nodes.name: Miners' Hut
nodes.description: The miners' hut is a humble dwelling with a glowing fire where a cheerful family gathers.

nodes.name: Holiday Attire
nodes.description: Holiday attire refers to the gaily decorated clothing worn by the people in the miners' hut during the Christmas gathering.

nodes.name: The Old Man
nodes.description: The old man is an elderly person in the hut, singing a Christmas song to his family. | The old man is a character who manages the fire and lamp in the parlour, and participates in the conversation.

nodes.name: The Old Woman
nodes.description: The old woman is the wife of the old man, part of the family gathered around the fire. | The old woman is one of the people grouped about the spoil, who laughs and comments on how the dead man frightened others away to profit them.

nodes.name: The Lighthouse
nodes.description: A lighthouse built on a reef, where two men watch the light and celebrate Christmas.

nodes.name: The Ship
nodes.description: A ship where the crew members hum Christmas tunes and have Christmas thoughts. | The ship is a vessel at sea where the Ghost and Scrooge observe the crew celebrating Christmas in their own way.

nodes.name: The Two Lighthouse Keepers
nodes.description: Two men who watch the light in the lighthouse and exchange Christmas greetings.

nodes.name: The Helmsman
nodes.description: The helmsman is the person at the wheel on the ship, part of the crew.

nodes.name: The Lookout
nodes.description: The lookout is positioned at the bow of the ship, among the crew.

nodes.name: The Officers
nodes.description: The officers are responsible for the watch on the ship, part of the crew.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Niece
nodes.description: Scrooge's niece by marriage is present at the Christmas gathering, laughs heartily, and responds indignantly to Fred's remarks about Scrooge. | Scrooge's niece is Fred's wife, who is described as very pretty and indignant at Scrooge's views. | Scrooge's niece is a relative of Scrooge who comments on his wealth and lack of patience with him, and she and others judge that he loses a very good dinner. | Scrooge's niece is the wife of Scrooge's nephew who encourages her husband to continue speaking and shares in the merriment. | Scrooge's niece is the hostess of the Christmas gathering and a skilled harp player. | Scrooge's niece is a character at the party who sits in a comfortable corner and participates in games, often defeating her sisters.

nodes.name: The Fire
nodes.description: The fire is a source of light and warmth built by two men on shore, shedding a ray of brightness on the sea.

nodes.name: The Two Men
nodes.description: Two men on the shore build a fire and exchange Merry Christmas wishes over a can of grog, representing the spirit of Christmas in remote places.

nodes.name: Wealth
nodes.description: Wealth is discussed in the context of Scrooge's riches being of no use to him because he does not use them for good.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Niece's Sisters
nodes.description: Scrooge's niece's sisters are relatives of Scrooge who agree with the niece's negative opinion of Scrooge.

nodes.name: Topper
nodes.description: Topper is a bachelor who expresses a view on marriage and has his eye on one of Scrooge's niece's sisters. | Topper is a guest at the Christmas party, known for his bass singing and his playful pursuit of the plump sister during games. | Topper is a character in a Christmas party scene, portrayed as a blind man who uses his supposed blindness to pursue a plump sister. | Topper is a character who could attest to the sharpness of the sisters in games. | Topper is a guest at the party, arriving after Fred.

nodes.name: Plump Sister
nodes.description: Plump sister is one of Scrooge's niece's sisters, who blushes when Topper makes a comment about bachelors. | The plump sister is a female character at the party whom Topper pursues, and she protests his unfair advances. | The Plump Sister is a participant who successfully guesses the answer in the game Yes and No.

nodes.name: Office
nodes.description: Office is Scrooge's workplace, described as mouldy, where Scrooge spends time in his own thoughts.

nodes.name: Fifty Pounds
nodes.description: Fifty pounds is a sum of money that Scrooge's nephew hopes Scrooge might leave to his poor clerk.

nodes.name: Uncle Scrooge
nodes.description: Uncle Scrooge is a miserly old man, the uncle of the narrator's wife, who is invited to Christmas dinner every year despite his grumpy demeanor.

nodes.name: The Plump Sister
nodes.description: The plump sister is a young woman at the Christmas party, wearing a lace tucker, who is pursued by Topper during the games. | The plump sister is a guest at the party, arriving after Topper.

nodes.name: The Christmas Party
nodes.description: The Christmas party is a festive gathering hosted by Scrooge's nephew and niece, featuring music, games, and merriment.

nodes.name: Harp
nodes.description: The harp is an instrument played by Scrooge's niece during the party.

nodes.name: The Air
nodes.description: The air is a simple musical tune that Scrooge's niece plays, familiar to the child who fetched Scrooge from boarding school.

nodes.name: The Boarding School
nodes.description: The boarding school is the place from which the child fetched Scrooge, as reminded by the Ghost of Christmas Past.

nodes.name: Ghost Of Christmas Present
nodes.description: The Ghost of Christmas Present is a spectral figure who shows Scrooge the party scene and is aware of Topper's deception. | The Ghost of Christmas Present is a spirit that sat in the corner of Scrooge's sitting-room.

nodes.name: Blind Man's Buff
nodes.description: Blind Man's Buff is a party game in which one player is blindfolded and tries to catch others, which Topper uses to pursue the plump sister.

nodes.name: How, When, And Where
nodes.description: How, When, and Where is a game played at the party, in which Scrooge's niece excels.

nodes.name: Forfeits
nodes.description: Forfeits is a game played at the party, involving penalties for mistakes, and Scrooge's niece participates.

nodes.name: Whitechapel Needle
nodes.description: A sharp needle from Whitechapel, used metaphorically to describe Scrooge's sharpness in guessing.

nodes.name: Yes and No
nodes.description: Yes and No is a game played where one person thinks of something and others ask questions to guess it.

nodes.name: How, When, and Where
nodes.description: How, When, and Where is a game in which the plump sister excels and beats her sisters.

nodes.name: Mulled Wine
nodes.description: Mulled wine is a drink prepared by Fred and the company for the toast to Scrooge.

nodes.name: Twelfth-Night Party
nodes.description: A children's party during Twelfth-Night that Scrooge and the Ghost attend, after which Scrooge notices the Ghost's hair has turned grey. | An event attended by Scrooge and the Ghost, where the Ghost's gray hair is first noticed.

nodes.name: Two Children
nodes.description: Two children, described as wretched and miserable, are brought out from under the Ghost's robe.

nodes.name: Almshouse
nodes.description: A location the spirit visits to leave his blessing and teach Scrooge his precepts.

nodes.name: Hospital
nodes.description: A location the spirit visits to leave his blessing and teach Scrooge his precepts.

nodes.name: Gaol
nodes.description: A location the spirit visits to leave his blessing and teach Scrooge his precepts.

nodes.name: Boy
nodes.description: The Boy is one of two children shown to Scrooge, described as wretched and wolfish, symbolizing ignorance. | A boy in Sunday clothes who is addressed by Scrooge, possibly loitering in the area. | The boy is a young character who is sent by Scrooge to purchase a turkey and bring the poulterer's man back.

nodes.name: Humanity
nodes.description: Humanity represents the collective condition of people, which is perverted in the children, as described by the Spirit.

nodes.name: Ignorance
nodes.description: Ignorance is a boy who symbolizes the societal ill of ignorance, described as having doom written on his brow unless erased.

nodes.name: The Last Spirit
nodes.description: The Last Spirit, also called the Phantom, is a solemn, hooded ghost that approaches Scrooge after the twelfth bell.

nodes.name: Prisons
nodes.description: Prisons are institutions mentioned by the Spirit as a rebuke to Scrooge's earlier words, symbolizing the lack of refuge for the poor.

nodes.name: Workhouses
nodes.description: Workhouses are institutions mentioned by the Spirit as a rebuke to Scrooge's earlier words, symbolizing the lack of real resource for the needy.

nodes.name: Old Jacob Marley
nodes.description: Old Jacob Marley is a deceased person who predicted the coming of the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come to Scrooge.

nodes.name: Ghost of the Future
nodes.description: The Ghost of the Future is a spectral being that Scrooge addresses, embodying the future and leading him through the City.

nodes.name: The Phantom
nodes.description: The Phantom is a spirit that leads Scrooge through the city, pointing to a group of business men. | The Phantom is a supernatural entity that Scrooge glances towards, likely the spirit guiding him through the scene. | The Phantom is a supernatural spirit that reveals scenes to Scrooge, using its dark robe to unveil a room with a family.

nodes.name: The Merchants
nodes.description: The merchants are business people in the City who are discussing the death of a man, noting that he has left money to his company.

nodes.name: The Business Men
nodes.description: The business men are a group of merchants in the City who are particularly engaged in conversation about a man's death and his money.

nodes.name: The Dead Man
nodes.description: The dead man is the subject of the business men's conversation, who died last night and left his money to his company. | The dead man is a deceased individual whose belongings are being distributed among the speakers, and who is criticized for his miserly nature. | The dead man is the subject of the dialogue and the body that lies plundered and bereft on a bare bed, unwatched and unwept. | The Dead Man is the departed individual whose life and death are the focus of Scrooge's vision. | The Dead Man is the person whose death is central to the scene. He was ill and dying when Scrooge tried to see him, and his death brings relief to Caroline and her husband.

nodes.name: The Man with the Large Chin
nodes.description: The man with the large chin is one of the business men who reveals he knows little about the dead man's affairs.
nodes.id: The Man with the Large Chin

nodes.name: The Red-Faced Gentleman
nodes.description: The red-faced gentleman is one of the business men who asks about the dead man's money.

nodes.name: Man With Large Chin
nodes.description: The man with the large chin is a speaker in the conversation who jokes about the funeral and claims to be the deceased's most particular friend.

nodes.name: Gentleman With Excrescence
nodes.description: The gentleman with the excrescence on his nose is a speaker who agrees to attend the funeral if a lunch is provided.

nodes.name: The Deceased
nodes.description: The deceased is the individual whose funeral is being discussed, left to his company.

nodes.name: First Businessman
nodes.description: First Businessman is a wealthy and important man of business who engages in a brief conversation with another businessman.

nodes.name: Second Businessman
nodes.description: Second Businessman is also wealthy and important, and reports the news about old Scratch's demise.

nodes.name: Christmas-Time
nodes.description: Christmas-Time is referenced as a season, with the weather being described as 'seasonable'.

nodes.name: Jacob
nodes.description: Scrooge's former business partner, whose death is referenced in the scene.

nodes.name: The Shadow of Scrooge
nodes.description: Scrooge's future self that he expects to see in the scene but does not find.

nodes.name: The Porch
nodes.description: The entrance to the place where people gathered, indicating a public area associated with Scrooge's habitual presence.

nodes.name: Phantom
nodes.description: The Phantom is an ethereal being accompanying Scrooge, with an outstretched hand and the ability to show scenes of the town. | The Phantom is a ghostly being who shows Scrooge the scene of a dead body, pointing steadily to the head of the corpse.

nodes.name: Unseen Eyes
nodes.description: The Unseen Eyes are the perceiving entities associated with the Phantom, looking at Scrooge keenly.

nodes.name: District
nodes.description: The District is an obscure, impoverished, and crime-ridden part of the town that Scrooge visited for the first time.

nodes.name: Low-Browed Shop
nodes.description: The Low-Browed Shop is a place where iron, rags, bottles, bones, and greasy offal were bought, and where the old man works.

nodes.name: Old Joe
nodes.description: Old Joe is a grey-haired, nearly seventy-year-old man who deals in the wares of the shop, smoking his pipe by a charcoal stove. | Old Joe is an old man who smokes a pipe and owns the shop where the three characters meet. | Old Joe is the person addressed by the woman to open a bundle and assess its value, indicating he is involved in the buying or valuing of stolen goods. | Old Joe is a buyer who purchases goods from women, noting their accounts on the wall and bargaining over prices. | Old Joe is a person who produces a flannel bag with money and tells out the gains of the group on the ground.

nodes.name: Charwoman
nodes.description: The Charwoman is the first woman who entered the shop with a heavy bundle, identitified by the others as the first arrival.

nodes.name: Laundress
nodes.description: The Laundress is the second woman who entered the shop with a heavy bundle, also surprised at the encounter.

nodes.name: Undertaker's Man
nodes.description: The Undertaker's Man is a man in faded black who entered the shop last, startled by the sight of the others.

nodes.name: The Charwoman
nodes.description: The Charwoman is the first of the three who entered the shop, and is described as being the first to be let alone.

nodes.name: The Laundress
nodes.description: The Laundress is the second of the three who entered the shop, and is described as being the second to be let alone.

nodes.name: The Undertaker's Man
nodes.description: The Undertaker's Man is the third of the three who entered the shop, and is described as being the third to be let alone.

nodes.name: The Parlour
nodes.description: The parlour is the space behind the screen of rags in old Joe's shop, where the three characters go. | The parlour is the space behind the screen of rags where the characters gather and converse.

nodes.name: The Shop
nodes.description: The shop is old Joe's place of business, with a door that skreeks and rusty hinges.

nodes.name: The Bundle
nodes.description: The bundle is a collection of items that the woman wants Old Joe to appraise, likely stolen from the dead man's house.

nodes.name: Man In Faded Black
nodes.description: A man dressed in faded black clothing who presents a small collection of valuable items for sale.

nodes.name: Plunder
nodes.description: Plunder refers to the stolen or found items brought by the man in faded black, including seals, a pencil-case, sleeve-buttons, and a brooch.

nodes.name: Household Items
nodes.description: Household items include sheets, towels, wearing apparel, silver teaspoons, sugar-tongs, and boots that Mrs. Dilber brought.

nodes.name: Dilber
nodes.description: Dilber is a woman who engages in selling items, including sheets, towels, clothing, silver teaspoons, and boots, to old Joe.

nodes.name: The First Woman
nodes.description: The first woman is a seller who brings a bundle containing bed-curtains taken from a deceased man's bed, along with blankets and oil.

nodes.name: Bed-Curtains
nodes.description: Bed-curtains are a large heavy roll of dark stuff that the first woman sells to old Joe, having taken them down from the deceased man's bed. | Bed-curtains are household items that Scrooge identifies as intact, symbolizing his opportunity to change the future.

nodes.name: Silver Teaspoons
nodes.description: Silver teaspoons are among the items sold by Dilber to old Joe.

nodes.name: Sugar-Tongs
nodes.description: Sugar-tongs are among the items sold by Dilber to old Joe.

nodes.name: Blankets
nodes.description: Blankets belong to the deceased man and are part of the bundle brought by the first woman.

nodes.name: Oil
nodes.description: Oil is a substance that the first woman warns Joe not to drop on the blankets.

nodes.name: The Deceased Man
nodes.description: The deceased man is the former owner of the bed-curtains, blankets, and other items sold by the first woman. | The Deceased Man is the former owner of the blankets and shirt; his body was dressed in the shirt, but the woman removed it.

nodes.name: The Shirt
nodes.description: The Shirt is a fine, hole-free garment that belonged to the deceased man. The woman removed it from his body before burial to prevent waste.

nodes.name: The Blankets
nodes.description: The Blankets belong to the deceased man and are being preserved, with the woman cautioning Joe not to spill oil on them.

nodes.name: Death
nodes.description: Death is portrayed as a powerful, cold, and dreadful force, but one that cannot diminish the goodness of a person's deeds.

nodes.name: The Mother
nodes.description: The Mother is a woman who is anxiously awaiting someone, likely connected to the dead man's death.

nodes.name: The Dark House
nodes.description: The Dark House is the empty room where the dead man lies, a place of death and desolation.

nodes.name: Caroline's Husband
nodes.description: Caroline's husband is a young man with a careworn and depressed face, who brings news of the man's death and reveals the possibility of hope due to the death.

nodes.name: Peter
nodes.description: Peter is a child in the Cratchit household who is reading a book. | One of Bob's children, who participates in the family conversation.

nodes.name: The Debt
nodes.description: A monetary debt that Caroline and her companion may owe, which might be transferred to a new creditor.

nodes.name: Sunday
nodes.description: Sunday is mentioned as a day when the sewing work would be completed, indicating a deadline or a special day in the household.

nodes.name: The Child
nodes.description: Bob Cratchit's child, referred to affectionately as 'My little child!' The child is present in a room upstairs, with a chair placed nearby.

nodes.name: The Green Place
nodes.description: A green place that Bob Cratchit visited and describes as refreshing, promising to walk there on Sundays.

nodes.name: Child
nodes.description: Bob's child, who is ill but present in the room upstairs.

nodes.name: Mr. Scrooge's Nephew
nodes.description: A kindly gentleman who met Bob on the street and showed concern for Bob's distress.

nodes.name: The Cratchit Daughters
nodes.description: The Cratchit daughters are the children of the Cratchit family who join in the family conversations and expressions of remembrance.

nodes.name: The Benefactor
nodes.description: The Benefactor is an unnamed gentleman who gave his card to Bob and expressed sympathy for the family, showing kindness.

nodes.name: Spirit of Tiny Tim
nodes.description: The Spirit of Tiny Tim is the essence of Tiny Tim, considered to be from God, a symbol of innocence and goodness.

nodes.name: The Churchyard
nodes.description: The churchyard is a burial ground where the grave of a man is located, overrun with grass and weeds.

nodes.name: The Grave
nodes.description: The grave is the specific burial site pointed out by the Spirit, which Scrooge approaches trembling. | The grave is Scrooge's own neglected burial site, pointed to by the Ghost, bearing his name.

nodes.name: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
nodes.description: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come is a spectral entity that shows Scrooge his future grave, pointing down to it silently.
nodes.id: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come

nodes.name: The Shadow of the Things
nodes.description: The shadows of the things that Will be or May be, representing possible future events.

nodes.name: Christmas Time
nodes.description: Christmas Time is referenced as a period of celebration and spiritual significance, praised by Scrooge.

nodes.name: The Bedpost
nodes.description: The Bedpost is the object that the Spirit transforms into, revealing Scrooge's own bed and room.

nodes.name: Saucepan
nodes.description: The saucepan is a household item that Scrooge notices in the fireplace area, part of his surroundings in his joy.

nodes.name: Ghost Of Jacob Marley
nodes.description: The Ghost of Jacob Marley is a spirit that entered through the door in Scrooge's sitting-room.

nodes.name: Wandering Spirits
nodes.description: The Wandering Spirits are spirits that Scrooge saw through the window of his sitting-room.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Sitting-Room
nodes.description: Scrooge's sitting-room is the room where Scrooge observes the locations associated with the spirits and expresses his joyful realization.

nodes.name: The Boy
nodes.description: The Boy is a young lad in Sunday clothes whom Scrooge questions about the day, and who knows the location of a poulterer's shop. | The boy is a young lad who knows the poulterer's location and confirms the turkey is still hanging there. | The boy is a young individual who is recompensed by Scrooge, likely for delivering the turkey.

nodes.name: The Spirits
nodes.description: The Spirits are supernatural beings who, in one night, have brought about Scrooge's transformation.

nodes.name: The Poulterer's
nodes.description: The Poulterer's is a shop on the next street, whose location Scrooge asks the boy about.

nodes.name: Poulterer's Shop
nodes.description: The poulterer's shop is located at the corner of the next street but one, where the prize turkey is sold.

nodes.name: Prize Turkey
nodes.description: The prize turkey is a large turkey, as big as the boy, hanging at the poulterer's and intended for purchase by Scrooge.

nodes.name: Turkey
nodes.description: The turkey is a large bird purchased by Scrooge to be sent to Bob Cratchit's family as an anonymous gift.

nodes.name: Joe Miller
nodes.description: Joe Miller is a person referenced by Scrooge as a comparison for the joke of sending the turkey to Bob's.

nodes.name: Poulterer's Man
nodes.description: The poulterer's man is the delivery person expected to bring the turkey to Scrooge.

nodes.name: Knocker
nodes.description: The knocker is a door knocker that Scrooge admires, expressing love for it after noticing it.

nodes.name: Bob Cratchit's House
nodes.description: Bob Cratchit's house is the destination where the turkey is to be delivered.

nodes.name: The Turkey
nodes.description: The turkey is a large bird that Scrooge buys and plans to send to Camden Town, noting it is too big to carry.

nodes.name: The Cab
nodes.description: The cab is a vehicle hired by Scrooge to transport the turkey to Camden Town.

nodes.name: The Ghost of Christmas Present
nodes.description: The Ghost of Christmas Present is a spirit that appeared to Scrooge earlier, and Scrooge recalls seeing people pouring forth as with this ghost.

nodes.name: The Girl (Maid)
nodes.description: The Girl is a servant in the nephew's household who answers the door and directs Scrooge to the dining-room.

nodes.name: The Dining Room
nodes.description: The Dining Room is the room in the nephew's house where the family is gathered and the table is set.

nodes.name: The Table
nodes.description: The Table is spread out in great array, indicating a formal meal setting in the dining room.

nodes.name: Fred's Wife
nodes.description: Fred's wife is Scrooge's niece by marriage, who is startled by Scrooge's sudden appearance.

nodes.name: Dining Room
nodes.description: The dining room is where the family is gathered, the table spread in great array for dinner.

nodes.name: Dinner
nodes.description: Dinner is the social gathering at Fred's home to which Scrooge has come.

nodes.name: The Office
nodes.description: The office is where the main character arrives early to catch Bob Cratchit coming late.

nodes.name: Total-Abstinence Principle
nodes.description: The Total-Abstinence Principle is a moral guideline that Scrooge follows after his transformation.

nodes.name: Spirits
nodes.description: Spirits are supernatural beings that Scrooge had no further intercourse with after his transformation.

Peter Cratchit is a son of Bob Cratchit. | Bob Cratchit suggests that the benefactor might secure a better situation for Peter, showing his hopes for his son. | Peter Cratchit shakes hands with Bob Cratchit during the family moment.
Tim Cratchit is the youngest son of Bob Cratchit.

Belinda Cratchit is a daughter of Bob Cratchit.

Martha Cratchit is a daughter of Bob Cratchit. | Martha playfully hides from her father, Bob, and then runs into his arms upon revealing herself. | Martha Cratchit hugs her father after revealing she was joking about not coming.
Bob Cratchit went down a slide on Cornhill in honour of Christmas Eve.
Bob Cratchit's dwelling is the home of Bob Cratchit, Scrooge's clerk.
The Ghost blesses Bob Cratchit's dwelling with his torch, signifying compassion for the poor.

Bob Cratchit is the patriarch of the Cratchit family and is the subject of concern and respect during Christmas preparations. | Bob Cratchit proposes a Christmas toast to the family, which they all re-echo. | The Cratchit family eagerly welcomes Bob home, helps him to his tea, and shows affection to comfort him. | Bob Cratchit addresses his family about remembering Tiny Tim and their first parting, and is met with affirmations and affection.
Bob Cratchit compounds a hot mixture with gin and lemons.
Bob Cratchit enters with the pudding, presenting it proudly to the family.
Bob Cratchit serves the compound from the jug to the family with beaming looks.

Bob Cratchit proposes a toast to Mr. Scrooge as the Founder of the Feast during their Christmas celebration. | Scrooge, with the Ghost, visits Bob Cratchit's house and observes the family. | Scrooge sends the turkey to Bob Cratchit without revealing his identity as the sender. | Scrooge raises Bob Cratchit's salary and promises to assist his family.
Bob Cratchit tells the family about a potential situation for Master Peter that would bring in five-and-sixpence weekly.
Bob says the work will be done long before Sunday, indicating the sewing work's deadline.
Bob Cratchit expresses deep emotional attachment to his child, calling the child 'My little child!' and breaking down in tears.
Bob Cratchit visited the green place and promises to walk there on Sundays, indicating his connection to the location.
Bob Cratchit is moved by the benefactor's kindness and shares the encounter with his family.
The Cratchit daughters kiss Bob Cratchit during the family moment.
The two young Cratchits kiss Bob Cratchit during the family moment.
Bob Cratchit is expected to arrive at the office, with the main character hoping to catch him being late.

Tiny Tim is mentioned as a brother whose absence is noted by his mother and is part of the family. | The Cratchit family all cry out that they will never forget Tiny Tim, showing collective remembrance.
The young Cratchit children help Tiny Tim by bearing him off to the wash-house to hear the pudding. | The two young Cratchits carry Tiny Tim to the wash-house and later escort him back to his stool.
Mrs. Cratchit is Tiny Tim's mother and asks about his behavior at church. | Mrs. Cratchit mentions Tiny Tim's illness and the effect on her eyes.
Tiny Tim hopes that people saw him in church because he is a cripple, thinking of those who made lame beggars walk.
Bob took Tiny Tim beside him at the table and interacted with him during the meal. | Bob is Tiny Tim's father, holds his withered hand, and is concerned for his well-being.
Tiny Tim was excited by the two young Cratchits and beat on the table with his knife.

Scrooge asks the Ghost of Christmas Present if Tiny Tim will live, showing concern for the child's fate. | Scrooge becomes a second father to Tiny Tim, who does not die. | Scrooge becomes a second father to Tiny Tim after his transformation.
The Ghost reveals a vision showing Tiny Tim's vacant seat and crutch without an owner, foretelling his death if shadows remain unaltered.
Tiny Tim drinks the toast to Mr. Scrooge but does not care about it, showing indifference to the toast.
Tiny Tim sings the plaintive song about a lost child with a small voice and performs it very well.
The Spirit's torch sprinkles brightness on the Cratchit family, and Scrooge especially observes Tiny Tim while accompanied by the Spirit.
The daughters join the family in vowing never to forget Tiny Tim.
The turkey is noted to be twice the size of Tiny Tim.
Peter Cratchit reads to the family, who listen quietly.
Scrooge hears Peter Cratchit reading and reflects on the words.

Mrs. Cratchit converses with Peter, asking about his father's arrival time and sharing memories of Tiny Tim. | Peter is teased by his mother about future prospects of settling down, leading to a light-hearted exchange.

Scrooge's nephew is identified as Fred when the plump sister guesses correctly.
Fred has mulled wine ready for the toast to Scrooge.
Fred is married to his wife, who is Scrooge's niece by marriage.
Topper arrives at the party and is warmly received, indicating a social connection with Fred.
The plump sister arrives at the party and is warmly received by Fred.
